title: RTGS: Real-Time 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM via Multi-Level Redundancy Reduction
problem: 3D Gaussian Splatting-based SLAM systems cannot achieve real-time throughput (>=30 FPS) on edge devices; even the most efficient 3DGS-SLAM algorithms run at 0.78–14 FPS on a state-of-the-art edge GPU (NVIDIA ONX). The rendering and backpropagation stages dominate runtime (>80%), with severe workload imbalance across pixels and costly atomic gradient aggregation causing memory conflicts.
motivation: Emerging AR/VR, autonomous driving, and robotics applications require real-time 3DGS-SLAM on power-constrained edge devices, but the gap between current algorithm throughput and the 30 FPS requirement exceeds 20x, blocking deployment.
method: RTGS is an algorithm-hardware co-design framework targeting 3DGS-SLAM. On the algorithm side: (1) adaptive Gaussian pruning progressively removes low-importance Gaussians by reusing gradients from the backpropagation pass (no added overhead for importance scoring), and (2) dynamic downsampling reduces non-keyframe resolution from 1/16 to 1/4 of full resolution based on temporal distance to nearest keyframe, reusing keyframe identification and alpha-computing results. On the hardware side, a plug-in ASIC integrated alongside edge GPU SMs includes: (1) a Workload Scheduling Unit (WSU) combining pixel-level pairwise scheduling with subtile-level streaming, exploiting inter-iteration workload similarity to reuse scheduling patterns; (2) a Rendering & Backpropagation (R&B) Buffer that stores forward-pass intermediate values (accumulated transmittance T and per-Gaussian color contributions) to eliminate recomputation during backpropagation, reducing alpha gradient latency from 20 to 4 cycles; and (3) a Gradient Merging Unit (GMU) using a Benes network and bypass-extended reduction tree to perform pipelined sparse gradient aggregation, replacing atomic-add operations with structured in-order merging. The design is implemented at 28 nm, 500 MHz, 8.11 W, 28.41 mm2.
key_novelty: Exploiting inter-iteration workload similarity in SLAM (where Gaussians are fixed between tracking iterations) to amortize scheduling overhead across iterations, enabling lightweight pixel-level pairwise scheduling that approaches oracle load balance with negligible cost.
contributions: Multi-level redundancy characterization of 3DGS-SLAM: identifying skewed Gaussian gradient distributions (14% of Gaussians drive 86% of gradient magnitude), high inter-frame pixel similarity in non-keyframes, and per-iteration workload stability
Adaptive Gaussian pruning that reuses existing backpropagation gradients for importance scoring with zero additional computational overhead
Dynamic downsampling that couples non-keyframe resolution scaling to keyframe distance, reusing keyframe identification and alpha-computing pipeline stages

RTGS ASIC plug-in with WSU (inter-iteration scheduling reuse), R&B Buffer (forward-to-backward data reuse eliminating recomputation), and GMU (Benes-network-based pipelined sparse gradient aggregation)
Up to 48.8x speedup and 82.5x energy efficiency over edge GPU baseline; real-time >=30 FPS achieved across four datasets and three 3DGS-SLAM algorithms

metrics.speedup: up to 48.8x over edge GPU baseline (ONX); real-time >=30 FPS on four datasets
metrics.energy_or_tops_w: up to 82.5x energy efficiency over edge GPU baseline
metrics.accuracy: ATE and PSNR within 10% variance vs. unmodified baselines
metrics.other: Gradient merging latency reduced 68% vs. atomic ops; alpha gradient compute reduced from 20 to 4 cycles

limitations: Hardware synthesized at 28 nm technology node, which is older than the 8 nm process used by the baseline edge GPU, making direct area/power comparisons less favorable; scaled 8nm projections show 2.40 mm2 / 3.76 W but are not validated with actual tape-out.
primary_theme: algorithm-hardware co-design for real-time 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM on edge
